source: Raynal, Clement, Gros, Sander (2026) Bridging the retrieval gap: familiar schema-governed categories support reminding of disparate events (Memory & Cognition 54:1965-1980)
finding: Large new human test of the 'retrieval gap' (Gick and Holyoak 1980, Gentner et al. 1993, Ross 1987/89). Exp 1 replicates the classic result: when a memory with both surface and structure match exists, it wins. Exp 2 pits pure surface matches against pure structure matches and structure wins by a wide margin when the cue is a familiar relational category. So 'people only retrieve by surface' is not universal.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=133): 502 memories; close analogs M=0.47 vs distant analogs M=0.09 per participant, t(132)=14.45, p<.001, d=0.84; 85.66% of recalls had surface overlap. Exp 2 (N=81): distant analogs M=0.46 vs surface-only matches M=0.04, t(80)=12.06, p<.001, d=0.82; 83.60% of 311 recalls had no surface overlap, 75.56% full structure. Exp 3: 411 memories, cues with no surface features retrieved more usual than unusual surface/structure combos.
quote: participants rely on highly familiar SGCs to process structural encodings and retrieve past experiences based on structural similarities
limits: Students, free recall of personal memories, familiar everyday relational categories (make an excuse, give up a resolution). Not problem-solving transfer. Retrieval of distant analogs depends on a well-formed category label for the cue. Exp 1 coded by one rater.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by structure is possible when the cue carries a familiar abstract relation label. Supports giving each stored subgoal a short relation label (what it does) and cueing with the same label vocabulary, not only raw text.

source: Spanish (Barcelona) team (2026) The effect of spatial structures on analogical problem solving (Fortress story to Radiation problem; PMC13253581)
finding: Conceptual re-run of the Gick and Holyoak Fortress-to-Radiation paradigm with Spanish undergraduates. Spontaneous transfer before any hint is rare (5 to 16 percent) and rises after a hint to the relevance of the story. Writing an analogous story first (analogy creation) lifts spontaneous transfer much more (43 to 63 percent). The original ~41 percent spontaneous and ~85 percent hinted figures were NOT reproduced in these conditions.
numbers: Study 1 (N=128, one Fortress story, summary task): standard story 3/64 correct before hint (5%), 20 more after hint, total 23/64 (36%); story without spatial cues 4/64 (6%), total 13/64 (20%); hint-stage difference chi2(1)=5.5, p=.02. Study 2 (drawing, N=104): before hint 8/50 (16%) vs 4/54 (7%); totals 50% vs 42%. Study 3 (invent an analogous situation, N=80): before hint 25/40 (63%) vs 17/40 (43%), chi2(1)=3.23, p=.072; totals 75% vs 60%. Incomplete story comprehension: 0% vs 31% solved (chi2(1)=6.93).
limits: Not an exact replication: one story not two, written summary first, Spanish translation, different hint wording, different scoring. The authors say the benefit emerged only after the hint, consistent with Gick and Holyoak. Cannot be used to say the 85 percent is wrong; it shows a single-story hinted rate of 36 percent in this design. The authors' name list was not recorded from the page.
agent_relevance: Hint and generating your own analogous case are the strong levers; passive exposure is weak. Suggests our agent should write a short restatement of the current subgoal in library vocabulary before lookup, rather than rely on the raw problem to cue a match.

source: Wang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: Neural theorem proving with growing libraries (arXiv 2310.00656)
finding: Closest published test of reuse at the subgoal level. Proofs are split into lemmas, each Isabelle-verified lemma is stored in a vector library and retrieved by embedding for later proofs. Removing the growing library (and the evolver that grows it) lowers pass rate on miniF2F-valid. Only about a quarter of solved problems used a retrieved skill.
numbers: miniF2F-valid, 50 attempts per problem, ChatGPT: with library 50.4%, without library 47.1% (+3.3 points); gap widens as the library grows. Best run 100 attempts: 57.0% valid, 50.0% test. Of 135 verified valid proofs, 24% used a retrieved skill; of those 51% copied the skill directly and 49% wrote a new lemma by imitation.
limits: Ablation also removes the evolver, so it is not 'retrieval only'. Compute is not matched: the library arm adds evolver calls (authors estimate 300 US dollars for one 100-attempt run). Single run, ablation only at 50 attempts on the validation set, no confidence interval. Authors note many miniF2F problems are trivial and need no skill. Verification is by the Isabelle checker, which is the strong admission gate.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is partly answered: a verified subgoal library gives a small, real, compute-uncontrolled gain in math proof. Admission by a formal checker is what makes a subgoal library safe; our agent needs an equivalent check (code run or answer check).

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ICML; arXiv 2401.16467)
finding: Compares a library of verified helper functions (subroutines) against a baseline agent that retrieves whole primitive programs from the SAME training data. Helper functions win on most domains, with the largest gains for small models. Ablations show the retry loop and the easy-to-hard curriculum matter more than pruning or editing the library.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B LOGO 45.6 to 57.1 (+11.5); GPT-3.5 Date 88.9 to 90.2; GPT-3.5 MATH +11.8; CodeLlama-7B TabMWP +11; TextCraft CodeLlama-34B 22.2 to 30.8 (ReAct GPT-3.5 25.6). Ablations on dev, CodeLlama-13B, 3 seeds (LOGO / Date / TextCraft): full 55.0 / 77.0 / 34.12; minus retry 48.3 / 51.9 / 30.43; minus curriculum 36.3 / 56.6 / 28.78; minus prune 52.0 / 65.5 / 25.26; minus edit 53.3 / 69.6 / 27.35. Lemur-70B on math: about equal to baseline within standard error.
limits: Library is built offline on about 200 training examples, then frozen; not online growth. Token cost of the retrieved helper block vs retrieved full programs is not equalized. Domains are structured (LOGO shapes, dates, Minecraft crafting) where shared subroutines obviously exist; math gains are smaller and noisier.
agent_relevance: Direct support for storing reusable verified subroutines instead of whole solved tasks, with a retrieval-matched control. The effect shrinks where no clear shared sub-structure exists (math).

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When not to trust language models: investigating effectiveness of parametric and non-parametric memories (ACL; arXiv 2212.10511)
finding: Tests a retrieval gate. Retrieval helps for rare (long-tail) facts and can HURT for popular facts the model already knows. A simple gate on subject popularity (retrieve only below a dev-set threshold) beats always-retrieve and never-retrieve, but only for large models; small models almost always need retrieval.
numbers: PopQA: for 10% of questions retrieval turned a correct unaided answer wrong (recall@1 0.14 on those vs 0.42 overall); for 17% retrieval fixed a wrong answer (recall@1 0.88). Best system: GPT-3 davinci-003 with adaptive retrieval (GenRead + Contriever) 46.5%, 5.3 points above any non-adaptive method. GPT-3 retrieves for only 40% of questions with BM25 under the gate; GPT-neox 20B under 20%. Gains small for models below 10B parameters.
limits: Factual QA with a popularity signal, not case reuse. The gate signal (Wikipedia page views) is external and not available for subgoals. Threshold chosen on a dev set per relation type.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 evidence by analogy: a gate on 'how much does the model already know this' beats always retrieving, and the optimum shifts with model size. Our agent could gate on a cheap self-solve attempt or on retrieval score instead of popularity; untested for subgoals.

source: Dong et al. (2025, v5 Feb 2026) Memory injection attacks on LLM agents via query-only interaction (MINJA; arXiv 2503.03704)
finding: An ordinary user can write wrong cases into an agent's long-term memory just by chatting, because agents admit their own query-and-output records without checking. The poisoned records are then retrieved for other users and the agent copies the bad reasoning (experience-following by force).
numbers: Average injection success rate 98.2% and average attack success rate 76.8% across agents and datasets (EHRAgent GPT-4 on MIMIC-III and eICU, RAP GPT-4o on WebShop, QA agents). ASR above 90% for GPT-4 EHR on eICU and GPT-4o RAP on WebShop; EHR MIMIC-III ASR falls 68.9% to 31.1% as benign records grow; utility drop on benign queries under 2% on three datasets, -10.0% on MMLU. Noisy retrieval barely helps defense: RAP ASR 97.8% to 95.6%.
limits: This is adversarial poisoning, not honest judge noise at 10 to 50 percent; it shows harm from wrong entries is large and cheap, but gives no dose-response curve. Defenses tested are limited. Authors' own agents.
agent_relevance: Strong reason for admission gating: unverified admission of stored cases is an attack surface and a noise source. The gap 3 dose-response (10 to 50 percent wrong) remains unmeasured.

source: Chen et al. (2024) AgentPoison: red-teaming LLM agents via poisoning memory or knowledge bases (NeurIPS; arXiv 2407.12784)
finding: Shows how few wrong cases are needed. An optimized trigger makes poisoned demonstrations get retrieved for triggered queries while benign queries stay normal.
numbers: Average attack success rate about 80% with under 1% drop in benign performance at poison rate under 0.1% of the memory or knowledge base, on a driving agent, a QA agent and EHRAgent.
limits: Attack requires write access to the store and trigger optimization against the retriever; not a model of natural error. A poison rate under 0.1% means the effect is retrieval hijack, not error share.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by embedding similarity is hijackable: a handful of wrong entries can dominate. Another reason to verify entries at admission and to cap how much any single case can steer an answer.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (ICML; arXiv 2302.00093)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to a grade-school math problem sharply cuts accuracy, most when the sentence overlaps in topic or role names. This is the cleanest measure of what a similar-but-useless retrieved case could do to a reasoning model. Instructions to ignore irrelevant text and self-consistency help; exemplars that themselves contain distractors help most.
numbers: GSM-IC: base-problem accuracy text-davinci-003 CoT 80.0, least-to-most 81.0. After one distractor, fewer than 30% of base problems are solved consistently across all distractor variants (macro accuracy). Role-overlap distractors push macro accuracy to 0 on problems with more than 2 reasoning steps for text-davinci-003. Self-consistency over 20 samples helped, yet for more than half of base problems the answer was still not consistently right.
limits: Older models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003), single sentence, synthetic distractors. Newer models are more robust, but the pattern (overlap hurts most) is the relevant one.
agent_relevance: A retrieved case that is similar in surface and wrong in structure behaves like a role-overlap distractor. Supports labelling retrieved cases 'reference, may not apply' and checking them against the current problem.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The power of noise: redefining retrieval for RAG systems (SIGIR; arXiv 2401.14887)
finding: High-scoring retrieved passages that do not contain the answer hurt the model more than random passages. Adding random passages next to the retrieved set can even raise accuracy. A relevant passage must still be present.
numbers: Natural Questions. Adding distracting (high-score, no-answer) documents cut accuracy by up to 0.38 (-67%) in some models; one distractor alone gave drops up to 0.24 (-25%). Adding random documents until the context was full raised Llama2 accuracy by up to 0.07 (+35%) with 4 retrieved documents. Replicated with BM25 and with Falcon.
limits: Open-domain QA, passage retrieval, 2023 models (Llama2 up to 4096 tokens). Mechanism of the random-noise benefit is unclear. Not case reuse.
agent_relevance: Near-miss retrievals are the dangerous kind. For subgoal lookup, K should be small and each retrieved item should have to pass a relevance check; a few unrelated items are not the main risk.

source: An et al. (2023) Skill-based few-shot selection for in-context learning (Skill-KNN; EMNLP; arXiv 2305.14210)
finding: Directly tests the retrieval key. Instead of embedding the raw problem text, the LLM first rewrites each problem as a short description of the skills needed (without surface words), and that description is embedded. This beats raw-text kNN on semantic parsing, with no training, and nearly matches an oracle that sees the gold output.
numbers: Spider, text-chat-davinci-002: best raw-input method (MMR with OpenAI Ada) 74.6% execution accuracy; Skill-KNN with SBERT plus distinctiveness 78.3%; oracle Target-KNN 78.6%. Skill-KNN with Ada 77.1 to 77.2%. Five datasets (Spider, Dr. Spider, KaggleDBQA, BIRD, COGS) and six models; best non-oracle on all. COGS compositional generalization shows the largest gains (Table 2 text columns scrambled by extraction, so only the trend is recorded). Comparable to fine-tuned retrievers (EPR, CEIL, TST) in Table 4.
limits: Skill descriptions come from a prompt with a few human-annotated demonstrations per task, so the key vocabulary is hand-seeded. Semantic parsing and SQL, not reasoning or planning. Surface-biased embeddings are the stated failure of raw-text keys.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 2: an abstract-skill key beats a problem-text key. For our library, store and search subgoals under an LLM-written skill description, with the raw text as fallback.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot in-context learning (NeurIPS; arXiv 2404.11018)
finding: Number of examples: with human-written solutions, MATH accuracy rises and then FALLS (peak near 125 examples) in Gemini 1.5 Pro. With model-generated solutions filtered for correct final answers (Reinforced ICL) accuracy plateaus near 25 examples, sits about 5 points higher, and does not fall at very large K. Prompts with problems only (no solutions) work about as well.
numbers: MATH500: ICL with ground-truth solutions peaks at about 125 examples then declines; Reinforced ICL plateaus at about 25 examples and is about 5% above ICL; 4-shot Minerva prompt 55.7% on MATH500 and 90.6% on GSM8K. Results averaged over five random seeds. The MATH prompt transfers to GSM8K.
limits: Examples are random or fixed, not retrieved by similarity; one model family; K counts examples not tokens. The correct-answer filter is the admission gate. No claim about small models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the best K depends on how consistent the examples are, not on a universal number. For a retrieved library, filter for verified correctness and keep K small; more only if examples are uniform.

source: Evo-Memory (2025, v2 May 2026) Benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory (arXiv 2511.20857), appendix multi-turn table, Gemini 2.5 Flash
finding: A third-party benchmark that re-implements AWM and Dynamic Cheatsheet next to a plain retrieve-raw-experience baseline (ExpRAG). The distilled-strategy methods (AWM, DC-Cu, DC-RS) land at the level of simply keeping history, while retrieving raw past experience (ExpRAG) is clearly better. On BabyAI, memory methods score below the no-memory baseline on success.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash, ALFWorld/BabyAI/PDDL/ScienceWorld average success/progress: Baseline 0.27/0.46; History 0.30/0.53; AWM 0.30/0.53; DC-Cu 0.29/0.53; DC-RS 0.30/0.54; ExpRecent 0.39/0.59; ExpRAG 0.46/0.63; ReMem 0.50/0.64. ALFWorld success: Baseline 0.12, History 0.28, AWM 0.26, ExpRAG 0.59, ReMem 0.66. BabyAI success: Baseline 0.61, History 0.52, AWM 0.52, ExpRAG 0.56, ReMem 0.53 (all memory below baseline).
limits: Evo-Memory authors implemented AWM and DC themselves in a streaming setup with their own prompts, so a weak result may reflect the port. Tables partly scrambled in text extraction; only cleanly parsed Gemini rows used. Single run, no intervals. This is a second non-author AWM run and it disagrees with AWM's own +12.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no independent evidence that distilled strategies beat raw retrieved cases; two third-party runs (ReasoningBank's, Evo-Memory's) show mixed to null results for AWM. Gap 6: memory can lower success when the environment gives no reusable structure (BabyAI).

source: Evo-Memory (2025) Table 3: memory with successes and failures both stored (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 3.7 Sonnet)
finding: When failed trajectories are stored without filtering, the plain raw-experience methods lose most of their gain. A method that reflects on and prunes its own memory (ReMem) keeps most of it.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash ALFWorld success with failures stored: ExpRecent 0.22, ExpRAG 0.25, ReMem 0.57, AWM 0.19, DC-RS 0.21; success-only equivalents (appendix table): ExpRecent 0.37, ExpRAG 0.59, ReMem 0.66, AWM 0.26, DC-RS 0.27. So ExpRAG falls from 0.59 to 0.25 (-0.34), below plain History (0.28) and about twice the no-memory baseline (0.12). Claude 3.7 Sonnet shows the same direction in the scrambled table.
limits: Not a dose-response: it is mixed success and failure versus success only, labelled by the environment. Table 3 text extraction was scrambled; Gemini numbers cross-checked against the appendix rows. Single run.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: unfiltered wrong cases can erase most of the retrieval gain of the simple method within one benchmark. Admission by verified outcome is not optional. The 10 to 50 percent curve is still missing.

source: Evo-Memory (2025) section 4.2.2: gain versus within-dataset task similarity
finding: ReMem's gain over the history baseline tracks how similar the tasks inside a dataset are to one another. Structured, repetitive environments (PDDL, ALFWorld) gain most; diverse reasoning sets (AIME-25, GPQA) gain little.
numbers: Pearson r = 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) between ReMem gain and average cosine distance to cluster center, across a handful of datasets.
limits: Correlation over few datasets, one similarity measure, no control for difficulty or ceiling. Not a test of what happens when a new item is dissimilar to every stored case.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 10: gains concentrate where tasks recur in structure; fresh, structurally different problems are where a library is least proven. Test our library on a held-out structure split.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning (ICML; arXiv 2402.17453), re-opened
finding: Re-read confirms the ablation: GPT-4 DS-Agent average best rank 2.08, without ReviseRank 2.58, without case-based reasoning 3.41 (lower is better; 12 development tasks, five trials). Detail: the removed piece is ReviseRank, which re-ranks and adjusts the retrieved case from execution feedback; the no-revise arm 'directly utilizes the top-ranked retrieved case without adjusting'.
numbers: Ablation GPT-4: 2.08 / 2.58 / 3.41. Development stage GPT-4 100% success; DS-Agent best on 9 of 12 tasks. Deployment stage (18 tasks, 10 runs, mean rank, lower better): GPT-4 zero-shot 28.2, one-shot 28.0, DS-Agent 12.7; GPT-3.5 30.8 / 35.0 / 17.1; Mixtral zero-shot 45.3, one-shot 39.4, DS-Agent 35.5 (equal to zero-shot on several tasks).
limits: Kaggle-style tabular and text tasks with a code executor; cases are human insights from Kaggle write-ups. Single ablation table with no intervals. Revision runs inside an iteration loop, so extra execution rounds, not equal compute.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: still a single setting. The re-read corrects one point: the ablation removes feedback-guided re-ranking and adjustment, a bundle, not 'copy vs adapt' alone.

source: Rubin, Herzig, Berant (2022) Learning to retrieve prompts for in-context learning (EPR; NAACL; arXiv 2112.08633)
finding: Retrieval by usefulness, not by similarity. A retriever is trained with labels from the LM's own probability of the correct output when a candidate example is in the prompt. It beats BM25 (similarity) and a case-based-reasoning scoring baseline on three semantic parsing sets, with one retrieved example as well as with many. Pure sentence-embedding similarity (SBERT) was worse than BM25 here.
numbers: Dev set, GPT-Neo 2.7B: BREAK LF-EM Random 1.7, SBERT 21.6, BM25 26.0, CBR (Das et al.) 25.7, EPR 31.9; MTOP EM 7.3 / 48.7 / 52.9 / 57.0 / 64.2; SMCalFlow EM 8.9 / 43.6 / 46.1 / 51.4 / 54.3. BREAK one-shot: BM25 15.2, CBR 14.5, EPR 23.0.
limits: Needs thousands of labelled training pairs and a scoring LM pass for each candidate; trained retriever is task-specific. Semantic parsing, not agents. Not the same as adaptation cost (Smyth and Keane), which measures how much a case must change, but it is the closest tested 'retrieve by use, not by look'.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, partial: ranking by measured helpfulness beats nearest-neighbour similarity by 5 to 8 points. Adaptation-guided retrieval itself remains untested on LLMs. A cheap online version: record which retrieved cases led to verified success and rank by that.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory (arXiv 2504.07952), Table 1 raw retrieval versus curated memory
finding: Same structured prompt, four memory variants. Dynamic Retrieval (DR) pastes the most similar raw past input-output pairs verbatim; DC-Cu and DC-RS keep curated summaries. Curated beats raw most of the time for GPT-4o, but raw retrieval can fall BELOW the memory-free prompt (DC-). The huge Game of 24 jump is the model storing a Python solver, a task with one reusable algorithm.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 (BL / DC- / DR / DC-Cu / DC-RS): 23.3 / 36.7 / 43.3 / 50.0 / 46.7. AIME 2025: 6.7 / 23.3 / 23.3 / 36.7 / 30.0. GPT-4o AIME 2024: 20.0 / 36.7 / 26.7 / 36.7 / 40.0 (DR below DC-). GPT-4o Game of 24: 10 / 19 / 6 / 93 / 99. GPQA-Diamond GPT-4o: 57.1 / 57.1 / 55.1 / 58.1 / 57.1. MMLU-Pro Eng GPT-4o: 53.2 / 51.6 / 48.8 / 44.0 / 51.2. Full-history append (FH) GPT-4o AIME 2024 fell to 6.7% vs 20.0% baseline. Authors say retrieval 'can introduce confusion, especially if suboptimal examples are recalled'.
limits: AIME sets are 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points; single run, no intervals. Authors' own method and baselines. Order effects (questions arrive in sequence). Memory is curated by the same model that answers, with no ground-truth check in the main setting.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 6: on tiny test sets curated beats raw, but raw retrieval was below the memory-free prompt in several cells. Gap 10: the dramatic gains come from a single discoverable algorithm (templated task), the opposite of fresh problems.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models (NeurIPS; arXiv 2406.04271)
finding: A library of distilled thought-templates is retrieved by embedding similarity between a distilled problem description and each template's description. Large gains concentrate on tasks where a template is effectively a program (Game of 24, Checkmate-in-One). Removing the meta-buffer lowers accuracy most on those two.
numbers: GPT-4 Table 1: Game of 24 standard 3.0, CoT 11.0, PAL 64.0, ToT 74.0, GoT 73.2, Meta-Prompting 67.0, BoT 82.4; MGSM 84.4 standard, 89.2 BoT; Multi-Step Arithmetic 84.0 standard, 99.8 BoT. Cost reported as about 12% of multi-query methods such as ToT. Ablation figures (problem-distiller, meta-buffer, buffer-manager) are plotted, not tabulated; direction only.
limits: Templates are task-type solvers, so this is reuse of a whole method, not a subgoal. Benchmarks are templated (Game of 24, Geometric Shapes, word sorting). No contamination test. Ablation numbers not read from a table. Not re-run by others here.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the strongest wins are on templated tasks; BoT shows nothing about structurally new problems. PAL at 64.0 shows a plain program-writing prompt already gets most of the Game of 24 gain.
